terms.def: A sculpted target you hit repeatedly to advance something — a monster, a building, a vehicle. Usually sits mid-playfield and often starts a multiball or mode when beaten.
A ball permanently trapped in a short lane; you hit your ball into it to register the shot. Often tied to power-up or lock features.
A target that falls flat when hit and pops back up later. Banks of drop targets often light locks, multipliers, or open shots hidden behind them.
A one-shot rescue — usually in the left outlane — that fires the ball back into play instead of letting it drain. Typically must be relit after each use.
A tight curling shot that circles behind the upper playfield features and returns quickly. Great for combos and often the fastest repeatable shot on a machine.
A shot around the outside edge of the playfield, entering one side and exiting the other (or returning the same way when a gate is closed).
The mushroom-shaped kickers that batter the ball around. Hits usually add small scores and sometimes advance features or spot lanes.

An elevated lane the ball climbs, returning to the playfield on a wireform or habitrail. In Pinball Genie a ramp shot's elevated portion draws as a dotted tail ending at a landing marker where the ball comes back down.
A switch the ball rolls across, most often the lettered lanes at the top of the playfield. Completing the set typically advances the bonus multiplier.
A shallow dish that holds the ball for a beat, awards something, then kicks it back out.
A hole shot that swallows the ball and ejects it elsewhere. Scoops commonly start modes, award mystery prizes, or serve as lock shots.
A hinged plate that spins as the ball passes through, scoring per rotation. A hard, clean shot makes it rip — several machines build big value on spinner rips.
A fixed flat target that registers a hit without moving. Banks of standups often light features when completed.
A row of related targets (drops or standups) treated as one feature — completing the whole bank is what usually matters.
A small raised playfield with its own flipper(s) and shots. Some ramps and locks deliver the ball up there.
A mechanism that fires the ball straight up out of a hole, usually onto a wireform or upper playfield.
The metal cover at the bottom of the playfield between and below the flippers, hiding the drain and trough area. Instruction cards live on it.
The upright cabinet section holding the display and artwork above the playfield.
A movable gate that changes where a shot delivers the ball — for example sending a ramp to a lock instead of its normal return. Some Pinball Genie goals note when a step rides the diverted path.
Losing the ball off the bottom of the playfield — between the flippers or down an outlane.
Your bats. Most machines have a left and right flipper at the bottom; some add upper or mini flippers for specific shots. Pinball Genie draws each shot from the flipper that actually makes it.
A hinged wire that lets the ball pass one direction only — how orbits feed lanes and how the shooter lane keeps balls from re-entering.
The lane just inside each outlane that returns the ball safely to a flipper. Ramps and wireforms usually feed an inlane — which is why the next shot starts from that flipper.
A light embedded in the playfield showing what is lit, running, or needed next. Reading inserts is most of reading a machine.
A smaller extra flipper mounted mid- or upper-playfield for specific shots, like a tight ramp or loop only it can reach.
The outermost lane on each side, which drains the ball past the flippers. Nudging and outlane saves are how you fight them.
The angled wooden surface everything is mounted on. Pinball Genie's map view is a straight-down schematic of it, with shots in normalized positions.
The spring rod (or auto-launch button) that puts the ball in play from the shooter lane. Short and full plunges reach different skill shots.

The channel on the far right where each ball starts. Pinball Genie draws plunges climbing the lane and arching over the top of the playfield — the one intentionally curved path, because the real ball follows the arch.
The triangular kickers just above each flipper that punch the ball sideways. They cause more chaos — and more outlane drains — than anything else down low.
A retractable post, often between the flippers or at a lane top, that pops up to hold or save the ball.
The elevated metal rail a ball rides after a ramp or VUK, delivering it to an inlane or flipper. Pinball Genie shows this elevated travel as the dotted tail after a ramp shot.

Shooting a target on the same side as the flipper holding the ball — the left flipper shooting the left ramp — instead of the usual cross-playfield angle. Some shots are safer or only makeable as backhands.
Letting the ball bounce off one lowered flipper across to the other instead of flipping at it — a controlled way to move the ball across.
Holding the ball at rest in the corner of a raised flipper. The foundation of control play: cradle first, then pick your shot.
Deliberately not flipping so a fast ball bounces off the lowered flipper and settles — often the safest response to a center feed.
Dropping a raised flipper just as the ball arrives so it lands dead on the flipper instead of bouncing away.

When you flip decides the angle. From the left flipper: flip early, while the ball is still near the heel, and the flipper carries it up its own side — the backhand window; flip late, with the ball out toward the tip, and it fires across the playfield. Every shot has a timing window, and learning them is most of learning a machine.

Keeping a flipper button pressed — to cradle a ball, to park one out of danger during multiball, or as the setup for skill shots that ask you to hold a flipper while plunging. Plenty of games also tuck secrets behind flipper holds in attract mode.

The standard cross-court swing: shooting a target on the opposite side of the playfield from your flipper — left flipper to right ramp, right flipper to left orbit. The contrast is the backhand, which shoots up the flipper's own side.
Catching a fast incoming ball by raising the flipper at the right instant so it sticks instead of rebounding.
Physically moving the machine — a controlled shove — to influence a rolling ball, save an outlane drain, or knock the ball off a post. Legal in moderation; too much tilts.
Shooting a moving ball without trapping it first. Faster and keeps the game flowing; riskier for the same reason. The controlled alternative is playing from a cradle.
Flicking a cradled ball off the flipper post to transfer it to the other flipper without losing control.
A partial pull of the plunger so the ball only just clears the lane — how many skill shots and controlled starts are made.
A hard, fast slap of both flipper buttons (often with a nudge) to save a ball headed straight down the middle.

A short, quick flick from a cradle that pops the ball over to the opposite flipper instead of shooting it — a controlled way to get the ball to the other side when the shot you want is a backhand away.
A tracked accomplishment in Pinball Genie's Achievements tab — check one off with a timestamp when you earn it on the real machine, and use its linked goal to see how to make it happen.
Earning an extra ball INTO a running multiball, extending it rather than the game.
A grace period after launch (or after certain events) where a drained ball is returned for free. The insert or display usually flashes while it is active.
Points totaled when your ball drains, built from what you did during the ball and multiplied by the bonus multiplier. On many machines it is a huge share of your score.
Hitting a defined sequence of shots back-to-back without stopping — ramps into loops into orbits. Pinball Genie's goal paths draw combos step by step.
An earned additional ball for your game, played after the current one drains. Light it, then shoot the lit shot to collect.
The machine's top recorded score. Beating any high-score entry usually earns free games or credits and lets you enter initials.
A prize that starts high and counts down fast — shoot the lit shot before it hits bottom to collect what remains.
The signature big award, usually during multiball. Building and collecting jackpots is the scoring heart of most modern machines.
Parking a ball in a holder toward starting multiball. Lock the required number and the next shot brings them all back at once.
A timed or objective-based mini-game — battle a villain, tour a location, complete a scene. Machines are largely structured as sets of modes leading to a wizard mode.
Two or more balls in play at once, normally with jackpots lit. Started by locks, bash toys, or mode progress depending on the machine.
A live boost to scoring: bonus multipliers raise your end-of-ball bonus, playfield multipliers raise everything while active. Stacking value under a multiplier is core strategy.
A grab-bag prize from a lit scoop or saucer — points, ball save, light extra ball, or something machine-specific.
A free game awarded for beating a set score (or by match at game end).
A precision award available on each ball launch — full or short plunge to a specific target. Pinball Genie draws plunge-fed skill shots from the shooter lane itself.

Pressing a flipper button to move which lane lamp is lit, so the ball's path collects the lit one. Many games rotate the top lanes this way, some only while the ball waits in the shooter lane, and some do not allow it at all - the machine's LIGHTS sheet says which.
A lit award, classically on the outlanes or a hard shot, worth a free game or big points when collected.
Getting multiple scoring features running at the same time — a mode inside a multiball under a playfield multiplier — so every shot counts several ways.
The elevated jackpot available after collecting the regular ones, usually the single most valuable shot of a multiball.
The penalty for nudging too hard: warnings first, then the ball (or game) ends with flippers dead. The bob inside the cabinet is the judge.
The climactic mode for completing a machine's major objectives — everything lit, huge scores, the reason to learn the rules. Most machines also have smaller mini-wizard modes along the way.
The machine's software, including its rules. Manufacturers update code over time, so a machine's rules can differ by installed version.

Pre-1978-era machines run on relays, steppers, and score reels instead of software — simpler rules, chime scoring, and pure shooting. Several classics in this app are EMs with intentionally lean goal lists.
The top production trim of a modern title — extra mechanisms, art, and features beyond the Premium, in a numbered run.
The middle trim of a modern title: the LE's mechanical features without the limited run. Some shots and rules differ from the Pro.
The base trim of a modern title — faster and simpler, sometimes missing mechanisms the Premium/LE have. Pinball Genie notes trim differences on affected shots and goals.
A licensed re-manufacture of a classic title with modern parts and displays. This app cites remade titles by their original maker and year.
The community-written document explaining a machine's rules in depth. Pinball Genie's goals distill rulesheet knowledge into shootable step lists — in our own words.
The microprocessor era that replaced EMs: electronic sound, digital displays, and software rules — everything from late-1970s classics to today.
Which version of a title a specific machine is (Pro, Premium, LE, or a remake). Pinball Genie tags shots and goals that only exist on certain trims.
